title: Random Pick with Blacklist
statement:
Write a class `Solution` that draws random integers from `0` to `n - 1` while avoiding a set of forbidden values.

- `new Solution(n, blacklist)` receives `n` and `blacklist`, a list of distinct integers from that range that must never be returned. At least one integer of the range is not in `blacklist`.
- `pick()` returns an integer in `[0, n - 1]` that is not in `blacklist`. Every allowed integer must be equally likely, and each call makes a new choice.

Try to call the random number generator as few times as possible (ideally once per `pick()`); `n` can be far larger than the blacklist, so listing every allowed value is too slow.

Use `Math.random()` for randomness; in this app it follows a fixed seed, so runs repeat exactly. Since many outputs are correct, an answer is accepted when the constructor gives `null`, every `pick()` result is an allowed integer, and across the calls of a case the results spread over the allowed integers about as evenly as a fair pick would (a generous statistical check).
constraints: All values of blacklist are distinct
At most 2 * 10^4 calls are made to pick (at most 499 per case here)
notes:
## Intuition

There are `size = n - blacklist.length` allowed integers. Rejection sampling (draw from `[0, n)` until the value is allowed) is fair but may need many draws when most values are banned, and listing every allowed value fails when `n` is a billion. Instead, draw one index uniformly from `[0, size)`. Most indices are allowed values themselves. The few that are banned get a stand-in: an allowed value from the upper part `[size, n)`, which the draw never reaches. The number of banned values below `size` equals the number of allowed values at or above `size`, so every banned low index gets its own partner and every allowed value is hit by exactly one index.

## Approach

1. Compute `size` and put the blacklist into the set `banned`.
2. Walk the blacklist with `last` starting at `n - 1`. Skip a value that is already `>= size`: the draw never produces it.
3. For a banned value below `size`, move `last` down past banned numbers, map the value to `last` in `remap`, and step `last` down once more so it is not reused.
4. In `pick()`, draw `index` from `[0, size)` with one call to `Math.random()`.
5. Return `remap.get(index)` if `index` is banned, otherwise `index` itself.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 7`, `blacklist = [2, 3, 5]`, so `size = 4` and `last = 6`. Value 2 is below 4 and 6 is allowed, so `remap` gets `2 -> 6` and `last` becomes 5. Value 3 is below 4; 5 is banned, so `last` drops to 4, giving `3 -> 4` and `last = 3`. Value 5 is not below 4 and is skipped. Now the indices 0, 1, 2, 3 produce 0, 1, 6, 4: the four allowed values, each with chance 1/4. LeetCode's sample `[null, 0, 4, 1, 6, 1, 0, 4]` is one possible sequence; the seeded run here makes its own.

## Complexity

- Time: O(B) for the constructor, where B is the blacklist length (`last` only moves down), and O(1) per `pick()`.
- Space: O(B) for `banned` and `remap`.

## Pitfalls

- Mapping a banned value to the next allowed value above it makes that neighbour twice as likely.
- The partner `last` must itself be allowed; skip banned numbers at the top before using it.
- Do not build an array of all allowed values: `n` can be `10^9`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `size` | how many integers are allowed; indices are drawn from `[0, size)` |
| `remap` | banned index below `size` -> allowed stand-in at or above `size` |
| `banned` | the blacklist as a set |
| `last` | the next candidate stand-in, moving down from `n - 1` |
| `value` | the blacklisted number being placed |
| `index` | the random draw in `pick()` |
